newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FEATURE - Indonesia seen making soft landing.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Indonesia seen making soft landing.

text.p: Indonesia's budget surplus in the just-concluded 1996/97 financial year is one of the signals that the country's economy is in good shape, but some minor adjustments are necessary, economists say.
The World Bank said Indonesia had succesfully made a soft landing in the 1996/97 fiscal year ending March 31, while posting a budget surplus of 817.9 billion rupiah ($340.8 million).
"On the macroeconomic side, we are quite satisfied with the way the government is managing the economy," Dennis de Tray, the World Bank representative in Jakarta, told Reuters.

"We continue to believe the government has done a good job in balancing fiscal and monetary instruments to achieve a soft landing," he said, adding that Indonesia, an oil exporter, was fortunate to have had strong global crude prices in the past year to back its policies.
The government's budgeted oil price for the fiscal year was $16.50 a barrel against the estimated realised average price of $20.76 per barrel.
ECONOMIC GROWTH, INFLATION AND CURRENT ACCOUNT DEFICIT
Indonesia, which embarked on a new budget on April 1, is likely to continue its prudent monetary and fiscal policies to maintain steady growth with low inflation, economists said.
"Inflation continues to trend downward and the current account deficit remains at an acceptable level...these are general signs the economy is easing off a bit," de Tray said.
Vincent Low, an economist at JP Morgan, agreed, adding that he expected the soft landing to continue into the new fiscal year.

"But it doesn't mean that the Indonesian economy is free of problems. Trade reform started off very strongly in 1996 but we haven't heard anything imminent yet," Low said, adding that domestic exports were already slowing down.
Economists said economic growth also indicated some cooling off, with GDP growth slowing down to 7.82 percent in the 1996 calendar year, compared with 8.21 percent in 1995.
But the current account deficit and inflation, both measures of overheating, were kept in check, they said.
The current account deficit rose to four percent of 1996/97 GDP from 3.4 percent in 1995/96, but it was forecast by the government to stay at four percent in the 1997/98 budget.
Inflation fell to 5.17 percent in the 1996/97 fiscal year from 8.86 percent in 1995/96.
GOVERNMENT SHOULD LOOK FOR ALTERNATIVE REVENUE SOURCES
Indonesia, following the modest budget surplus in 1996/97, revised its budget to 95.84 trillion rupiah ($40 billion) from 90.6 trillion rupiah ($37.7 billion) set initially.
But economists said they were not entirely happy with the dependence on oil.

"We were a little concerned about the fact that the nature of the budgetary surplus generated last year was perhaps a little too dependent on higher oil prices and less based on domestic resource mobilisation," de Tray said.

He suggested the government improve its tax base and revisit some of the specific elements of the tax codes. The government has said indirect tax collection such as value added tax and import duties were below initial targets.
He also suggested that forestry royalties should be increased to boost government revenue.
GROWTH IN CREDIT, MONEY SUPPLY SEEN WORRYING
Although the prudent policies managed to contain inflation, credit growth and monetary goals exceeded government targets.

Broad M2 money supply growth was about 30.51 percent in January year-on-year against 17 percent set in the 1996/97 budget. Credit growth expanded by around 24 percent in January, compared with the 16-percent target.

Dominique Maire, an economist at UBS Global Research, said easy funding and strong capital inflows were responsible for overshooting targets, and suggested a further slowdown in credit and demand in the wake of weaker non-oil export performance.

The central bank, unhappy with the overshooting, raised its reserve requirement rate to five percent from three percent effective from April 16 and called on banks to be more prudent in their credit policy.
"The bank has no choice but to tighten policy," Maire said.
Low, however, pointed out that tight monetary policy in the past had beaten down domestic demand growth.
"We remain fairly bullish on Indonesia," he said.
TIGHTENING FISCAL TOOLS TO ALLOW MONETARY POLICY TO EASE
De Tray suggested the government enhance its fiscal tools to reduce the weight of monetary policy.

"Indonesia may perhaps want to shift a little more reliance on to the fiscal side of the equation so that it can afford to put less weight on the monetary policy," he said, adding that a reliance on monetary policy in an open economy brought with it a variety of difficulties, including an appreciating exchange rate and high interest rates.
De Tray said over time these variables needed to decline slightly and the alternative was using fiscal measures to push through policy.
"This would dampen a bit the recent rapid foreign exchange inflows which put some upward pressure on the rupiah," he said.
Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves have risen to almost $20 billion in February from $15.96 billion in February 1996.
Low forecast another 75 basis points cut of the short-term discount rate, the benchmark rate for lending money from Bank Indonesia, within the next six months.
The discount rate has been cut twice since December 1996.
BANK INDONESIA HAS CURRENCY MANAGEMENT WELL UNDER CONTROL
Low said another way of allowing the economy to adjust to rising capital inflows was through the widening of the exchange rate band, which has also been widely expected.
"But the problem now is the export growth. We think there won't be any widening until the export picture recovers. It doesn't make sense now," he said.
The Indonesian rupiah has appreciated against the dollar each time the central bank widened its currency band.
De Tray said Indonesia seemed to have its management of the rupiah well under control.
"Bank Indonesia has done a good job of increasing, shall we say, the shock absorber that the economy now has to withstand in both domestic and international shocks," de Tray said.
"That is a good thing and at the moment it (the bank) has quite a lot of latitude on the management of the rupiah."
POLITICAL RISKS IN AN ELECTION YEAR

Jacob Stott, managing director of JP Morgan in Singapore, told Reuters while in Jakarta last month at the head of a bank consortium providing a $500 million stand-by facility to Bank Indonesia, that domestic political risks were not worrying.
"I feel pretty good about the political risks," Stott said when asked about the general election scheduled on May 29 and presidential elections next year.

"I think the markets have to deal with uncertainties of various kinds. Here is an uncertainty and therefore a risk. I don't think it's something for banks to worry about to such an extent that transactions like this can't be done," he said.
"As long as the risks are properly placed, it's better to absorb those risks," Stott said.
De Tray said investors' confidence remained strong and people were certainly aware of the elections.

"We are not anticipating a major disruption in investment into Indonesia through the election period although I certainly expect there might be some slowdown as people watch what is happening," de Tray said.
